asDecan.p: Nobody's in the picture on the Eight of Wands. Eight wooden staves cross an empty sky at the same angle, already dropping toward wherever they'll land. Your Sun is in the first ten degrees of Sagittarius, and in the Golden Dawn order Mercury rules that stretch. Sagittarius is mutable fire, ruled by Jupiter, the sign of the long view, and this opening slice is where it's freshest. Mercury's home is Gemini, straight across the zodiac, so here it's in detriment. In practice that's a planet that likes exact wording and small print, working in a sign that only wants the headline, so it has to try harder here than it would at home. The Moon takes the next ten degrees, the Nine, where the sign's been knocked about and is guarding what it's got. Saturn has the last ten, the Ten, carrying far too much. Yours comes before any of that. Temperance is still your Sun card. The Eight just narrows it down.

In a meeting you're usually three steps ahead of whoever's presenting and already asking about slide nine. At a family dinner you'll start a story about a trip to Lisbon, wander off into the history of the trams, and come back twenty minutes later to find everyone's on dessert. You read the first chapter of four books in the same week and have opinions on all of them. A friend texts a simple yes-or-no question and gets a six-minute voice note back. Mercury in Sagittarius is quick and very sure of itself, and it tends to reach the conclusion before the evidence has quite caught up. Most of the time you land on your feet anyway, to be honest, and you know it, which is why you'd book the flight and sort out the details once you're there.

The thing people don't always credit you with is that you can explain things. Mercury can't keep hold of every detail in this sign, so over the years you've learnt to pick out the one detail that matters, and it turns out that's most of what explaining is. Sit you next to a friend panicking over a tax form, or a fourteen-year-old who can't see the point of algebra, and you'll find the sentence that makes it click. You're often the one the family rings when a letter from the council makes no sense. You also get bored of bad news quickly, which sounds like a flaw and mostly isn't. After a rough week you're the one in the group chat who's already found something funny in it, and your friends rely on that more than they'd say.

The quieter problem is that you pass things on before you've checked them. Mercury in detriment gets the gist right and the specifics wrong, so you'll state a fact at a dinner party with total confidence and realise on the drive home it was a different country, or a different decade. Mostly that's harmless. It stops being harmless when the fact is about a person. You'll tell a friend what you reckon their partner meant, or sum up a colleague to your boss in one breezy line, and that line follows them around for months. There's a bluntness in it too that you honestly don't hear. Someone shows you the new haircut, you tell them what you think, quickly and cheerfully, and then you can't work out why they've gone quiet for the rest of the night.

When something goes wrong your first move is to talk. You ring three people in an hour and tell it a slightly different way each time, looking for the version that makes sense. Then the plans start, usually big ones, a new job, a move interstate, a course in something you've never mentioned before. A week later there are six plans, none of them started, and you're lying awake at two in the morning running through all of them. The people closest to you have heard the story so often they've stopped really listening, and they can tell your mind is somewhere else when you're with them. What helps is getting your body moving and your mouth quiet for a while. A long walk with no podcast in your ears. Then pick one of the plans and do its first dull step.

You fall for people who can keep up with you in conversation, and a first date can easily run to four hours and three venues. What's less obvious is how much you need things said straight. Hints go right past you. A partner who sighs and says it's fine will be believed, cheerfully, for weeks, and then you're genuinely hurt to find out it was never fine. Mercury in this sign takes words at face value and moves on. You also need time off on your own, a weekend away with a mate, an evening at a lecture on Roman roads, and you come back warmer for it. The trouble starts when you forget to mention you're going. Send a text before you leave, even a short one from the airport.

You do best where you're allowed to move about and talk to people. Publishing, tourism, sales across time zones, anything with an international desk or a conference circuit. A job that keeps you at the same screen doing the same checks every day will wear you down within a year, and you'll be drafting your resignation in your head during the Monday stand-up. You're very good in the first week of a project, when nobody's sure what it is yet and someone has to write the pitch. By the ninth month, when the contract has to be read line by line, you're weaker. That's the detriment, and it's fine as long as you know it. Find the colleague who loves fine print and make a friend of them, and let them check your numbers before anything goes to the client.

At twenty this slice of Sagittarius is usually all motion. Backpacking, two degrees started and one finished, strong opinions about countries you spent four days in. You're funny and good company and hard to pin down, and what you want to do with your life changes every six months or so. By the mid-thirties most people with this decan have learnt, often the embarrassing way, that being quick and being right are separate skills, and they start checking. The speed stays. What changes is that you ask one more question before you give an opinion. The fifties tend to bring a bit of authority, since people have noticed your explanations hold up. A lot of early Sagittarians I've seen end up teaching in some form, or leading the kind of tour they used to tag along on.

Before you send any message that says something about another person, an email to your manager, a text in the family chat, a voice note about a friend's break-up, wait as long as it takes the kettle to boil. Then read it through once and check one fact in it. Just one, a name, a date, what they actually said. If it holds up, send it. If it doesn't, fix that line and leave the rest alone.
